topic: Physics — Forces and motion: Describing motion along a line
subject: combined-science

items.q: A student walks 30 m due east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the point where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?
items.correct: Distance 60 m; displacement zero, as she ends where she began
items.misconception: Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m, as both measure her walk
items.why: Both quantities are lengths in metres, and in the first examples students meet - a single straight walk from A to B - the two numbers really are equal, so the difference never has to be noticed. Distance is measured along the whole path travelled; displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish and includes direction. Out and back gives 60 m of distance but zero displacement.
items.random_wrong: Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m, the furthest point reached

items.q: A walker sets off from a car park, goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. Which of these correctly expresses her displacement from the car park?
items.correct: 5.0 km, in a direction 37 degrees east of north
items.misconception: 7.0 km, on a heading 37 degrees east of north
items.why: Adding is what students do with distances, and the two legs are given in the same unit, so arithmetic addition feels like the obvious move. Displacements at right angles combine like the sides of a right-angled triangle, not by simple addition. Here the magnitude is 5.0 km and the direction must be stated as well.
items.random_wrong: 5.0 km, and no direction needs to be stated

items.q: Which pair contains only scalar quantities?
items.correct: Distance and speed, as neither has a direction
items.misconception: Speed and velocity, as both describe how fast it goes
items.why: In everyday English the two words are used as synonyms, and in most simple problems only one direction of travel is considered, so nothing forces the distinction. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Equal speeds in opposite directions are different velocities.
items.random_wrong: Distance and displacement, as both are lengths in metres

items.q: Which quantity is only fully described when a direction is given as well as a number and a unit?
items.correct: Displacement, a vector quantity
items.misconception: Distance, measured along the path
items.why: Both quantities are lengths in metres, and in the first examples students meet - a single straight walk from A to B - the two numbers really are equal, so the difference never has to be noticed. Distance is measured along the whole path travelled; displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish and includes direction. Out and back gives 60 m of distance but zero displacement.
items.random_wrong: The time taken, measured in seconds

items.q: Two cars travel along the same straight road at 20 m/s, one heading north and the other heading south. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Their speeds are equal but their velocities differ
items.misconception: Their speeds and their velocities are both equal
items.why: In everyday English the two words are used as synonyms, and in most simple problems only one direction of travel is considered, so nothing forces the distinction. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Equal speeds in opposite directions are different velocities.
items.random_wrong: Their speeds differ, but their velocities match

items.q: Why is the speed of a car driven across a busy town rarely constant?
items.correct: The driver keeps changing speed at junctions and bends
items.misconception: Cars are built to hold a single steady speed once moving
items.why: Textbook problems nearly always specify a constant speed so that s = v t can be used, so students come to treat constant speed as the normal case rather than a simplification. Real journeys involve constant changes of speed, which is why average speed - total distance divided by total time - is needed.
items.random_wrong: Speed can only change when the direction changes too

items.q: Which list gives factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?
items.correct: Age, fitness, terrain and the distance travelled
items.misconception: Fitness alone, as everybody else walks at 1.5 m/s
items.why: Textbook problems nearly always specify a constant speed so that s = v t can be used, so students come to treat constant speed as the normal case rather than a simplification. Real journeys involve constant changes of speed, which is why average speed - total distance divided by total time - is needed.
items.random_wrong: Terrain and distance only, as age has no effect on it

items.q: Which is the best estimate of the typical speed of a person walking?
items.correct: 1.5 m/s, or about 5 km/h
items.misconception: 6.0 m/s, close to 22 km/h
items.why: The typical values are learned as a list of three numbers with no physical anchor, so which number belongs to which activity is easily swapped. The typical values increase in the order walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s - each roughly double the one before.
items.random_wrong: 15 m/s, or roughly 54 km/h

items.q: A student is asked to use typical values for the speeds of a runner and a cyclist. Which pair should she use?
items.correct: Running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s
items.misconception: Running about 6 m/s, cycling about 3 m/s
items.why: The typical values are learned as a list of three numbers with no physical anchor, so which number belongs to which activity is easily swapped. The typical values increase in the order walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s - each roughly double the one before.
items.random_wrong: Running near 3 m/s, cycling near 3 m/s

items.q: Which is the most sensible typical speed to quote for a car travelling along a motorway?
items.correct: About 30 m/s, which is roughly 70 miles per hour
items.misconception: About 300 m/s, which is close to the speed of sound
items.why: Students have little feel for the size of metres per second and do not check the value against experience, so an answer ten times too large passes unnoticed. Typical values are walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s; 15 m/s is closer to a car in a town.
items.random_wrong: About 10 m/s, a little faster than a cyclist

items.q: Which statement about the speed of sound in air is correct?
items.correct: It varies, but a typical value is 330 m/s
items.misconception: It is fixed at 300 000 000 m/s in every case
items.why: Sound seems to arrive instantly over short distances, and 'the speed of sound' is spoken of as though it were one unchanging constant. A typical value is 330 m/s, but the speed of sound in air varies, for example with temperature, just as the speed of the wind varies.
items.random_wrong: It is always exactly 330 m/s, whatever the air

items.q: A student sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 6.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away was the lightning?
items.why: Students remember the triangle of letters rather than the equation, and the unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to forget once the arithmetic starts. Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Always convert the distance to metres first when the speed is in m/s.

items.q: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s. How long does it take to travel 9.0 km?
items.why: Students remember the triangle of letters rather than the equation, and the unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to forget once the arithmetic starts. Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Always convert the distance to metres first when the speed is in m/s.

items.q: A student wants to measure the average speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp. Which method should she use?
items.correct: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide distance by time
items.misconception: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then multiply these
items.why: Students remember the triangle of letters rather than the equation, and the unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to forget once the arithmetic starts. Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Always convert the distance to metres first when the speed is in m/s.
items.random_wrong: Measure the distance and the time, then divide the time by the distance

items.q: A car's speed changes constantly during a journey through town. How should its average speed for the journey be found?
items.correct: Divide the total distance travelled by the total time taken
items.misconception: Add together the highest and the lowest speeds, then halve that
items.why: The word 'average' triggers the arithmetic mean learned in maths, and it happens to give the right answer in the special case where the two stages take equal times. Average speed for non-uniform motion is total distance travelled divided by total time taken, counting any stops as part of the time.
items.random_wrong: Divide the total time taken by the total distance moved

items.q: A cyclist rides 4.0 km in 500 s, rests for 100 s, and then rides 5.0 km in 400 s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?
items.why: The word 'average' triggers the arithmetic mean learned in maths, and it happens to give the right answer in the special case where the two stages take equal times. Average speed for non-uniform motion is total distance travelled divided by total time taken, counting any stops as part of the time.
items.random_wrong: 10 m/s

items.q: Which statement best describes the velocity of a moving object?
items.correct: Speed in a given direction
items.misconception: Simply another word for speed
items.why: In everyday English the two words are used as synonyms, and in most simple problems only one direction of travel is considered, so nothing forces the distinction. Velocity is speed in a given direction. Equal speeds in opposite directions are different velocities.
items.random_wrong: How far it travels each second

items.q: Which statement correctly classifies distance, displacement, speed and velocity?
items.correct: Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors
items.misconception: Distance and displacement are scalars, with the others vectors
items.why: Both quantities are lengths in metres, and in the first examples students meet - a single straight walk from A to B - the two numbers really are equal, so the difference never has to be noticed. Distance is measured along the whole path travelled; displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish and includes direction. Out and back gives 60 m of distance but zero displacement.
items.random_wrong: Distance and velocity are scalars, displacement and speed vectors

items.q: A car is driven round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement about its motion is correct?
items.correct: Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
items.misconception: Both its speed and its velocity stay constant all round
items.why: Nothing about the motion looks like it is changing - the speedometer reading never moves - and students track the number rather than the direction. Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even when the speed stays the same. Circular motion at constant speed has constantly changing velocity.
items.random_wrong: Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing

items.q: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph tell you about the object?
items.correct: The speed at that moment
items.misconception: The acceleration at that time
items.why: Both graphs have time along the bottom, so students transfer the distance-time rule - gradient is speed - to the velocity-time graph without re-deriving it. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is the acceleration.
items.random_wrong: The distance moved so far

items.q: On a distance-time graph a straight line passes through the origin and through the point (8.0 s, 120 m). What is the speed of the object?
items.correct: 15 m/s
items.why: The vertical axis carries the only number that looks like an answer, and students who have not internalised gradient as rise over run take the coordinate itself. Speed is the gradient of a distance-time graph - the change in distance divided by the change in time - not the value of the distance at a point.

items.q: Part of a distance-time graph for a car is a horizontal straight line. What is the car doing during that part?
items.correct: It is stationary and staying put
items.misconception: It is moving at a steady speed there
items.why: Students read 'straight line' as 'steady motion' without looking at the gradient, and a flat line does look like a smooth, unchanging journey. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. Zero gradient means zero speed; a sloping straight line means constant speed.
items.random_wrong: It is going back towards the start

items.q: The distance-time graph for an accelerating car is a curve. How should the speed of the car at 6 s be found?
items.correct: Draw a tangent to the curve at 6 s and measure its gradient
items.misconception: Join the origin to the point at 6 s and find that gradient
items.why: The origin-to-point line is what works for a straight graph through the origin, so students carry the method across to a curve without noticing that it now gives an average, not an instantaneous, speed. For a curved graph the origin-to-point line gives the average speed up to that time. The speed at that instant is the gradient of the tangent drawn at the point.
items.random_wrong: Read the distance at 6 s straight off the vertical axis

items.q: On a distance-time graph the line curves upwards and becomes steeper as time goes on. What does this show?
items.correct: The object is speeding up as time goes on
items.misconception: The object is slowing down as time goes on
items.why: Students read 'straight line' as 'steady motion' without looking at the gradient, and a flat line does look like a smooth, unchanging journey. On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. Zero gradient means zero speed; a sloping straight line means constant speed.
items.random_wrong: The object moves at a steady high speed

items.q: A motorbike speeds up from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its average acceleration?
items.why: Students recall the equation as 'velocity over time' and the final velocity is the number most visible in the question, so the initial velocity is quietly dropped. Acceleration = (change in velocity) / (time taken). The change in velocity is final minus initial, here 29 - 5 = 24 m/s.

items.q: A train slows down uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 40 s. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It is decelerating, and so its acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2
items.misconception: It is now travelling backwards along the track at 10 m/s
items.why: The minus sign is read as a direction of travel rather than as the direction of the change in velocity, especially when signs are met before vectors are secure. An object that slows down is decelerating. The acceleration points opposite to the velocity, but the object keeps moving forwards until its velocity reaches zero.
items.random_wrong: It is decelerating at 0.25 m/s^2, from 10 m/s in 40 s

items.q: Which is the best estimate of the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights?
items.correct: About 2 m/s^2, reaching some 12 m/s in about 6 s
items.misconception: About 100 m/s^2, so reaching 12 m/s in around 0.1 s
items.why: Students have no reference points for accelerations, and a car pulling away feels dramatic, so any large number seems as good as another. Check an estimate by multiplying: 2 m/s^2 for 6 s gives 12 m/s, which is a sensible town speed. 100 m/s^2 would reach that speed in about a tenth of a second.
items.random_wrong: About 9.8 m/s^2, the same as an object falling

items.q: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?
items.correct: The object's acceleration
items.misconception: The distance it has travelled
items.why: Both graphs have time along the bottom, so students transfer the distance-time rule - gradient is speed - to the velocity-time graph without re-deriving it. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is the acceleration.
items.random_wrong: The speed it has at that moment

items.q: A velocity-time graph for a cyclist is a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance does the cyclist travel in that time?
items.why: Both graphs have time along the bottom, so students transfer the distance-time rule - gradient is speed - to the velocity-time graph without re-deriving it. On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is the acceleration.

items.q: A car accelerates uniformly at 3.5 m/s^2 from an initial velocity of 24 m/s over a distance of 7.0 m. What is its final velocity?
items.correct: 25 m/s
items.why: The equation is the only one on the sheet with squared terms, and the final step of square rooting is easy to forget once a large number has been produced. Use v^2 - u^2 = 2as to find v^2, then take the square root. Both velocity terms are squared, so the initial velocity cannot be dropped.

items.q: A ball is dropped near the Earth's surface. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration as it falls?
items.correct: About 9.8 m/s^2, directed downwards
items.misconception: About 9.8 m/s^2 if the ball is heavy
items.why: The heavier ball does have a larger weight, and students link larger force to larger acceleration without allowing for its larger mass as well. Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, independent of mass.
items.random_wrong: About 9.8 m/s, growing as the ball falls

items.q: A skydiver falling through the air reaches terminal velocity. Which statement describes what is happening?
items.correct: The resultant force is zero, so velocity is steady
items.misconception: Gravity has stopped acting, so no force acts at all now
items.why: Students associate 'no acceleration' with 'no forces' rather than with balanced forces, so the simplest explanation is that one of the forces has switched off. At terminal velocity the weight and the drag force are equal and opposite. Both forces are still acting; it is the resultant that is zero.
items.random_wrong: The skydiver slows down and stops falling in the air

items.q: A ship sails 12 km from a harbour and ends up due south of it. How should its displacement be written?
items.correct: 12 km due south of the harbour - the magnitude and the direction are both needed.
items.misconception: Writing '12 km' on its own is a complete answer for a displacement.
items.why: Almost every number a student writes in science is a magnitude and a unit, so the habit of stopping there is very strong, and a direction feels like extra description rather than part of the value. A displacement is a vector, so it is only fully expressed when both the magnitude and the direction of the straight line from start to finish are given.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is speed a scalar or a vector quantity?
items.correct: Speed is a scalar quantity, because it does not involve direction.
items.misconception: Speed must be a vector because a moving object is obviously going somewhere.
items.why: Students confuse the direction the object happens to be travelling with whether direction is part of the quantity itself. A car has a direction, but its speedometer reading does not. Speed tells you only how fast, never which way; that makes it a scalar. Velocity is the vector that carries the direction as well.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance is travelled?
items.correct: 60 m, the area of the triangle: half of 8.0 s multiplied by 15 m/s.
items.misconception: 120 m, from base multiplied by height, with the factor of one half left out.
items.why: Rectangles are the first areas students meet under a velocity-time graph, and the triangle rule is applied without noticing that the shape has changed. The area of the triangle under the line is half the base times the height. Where the shape is awkward, the area can be measured by counting squares.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does a velocity-time graph look like for an object that reaches terminal velocity?
items.correct: It rises steeply at first, curves as the gradient falls, then levels off as a horizontal line.
items.misconception: The line rises and then falls back to zero, because the object slows to a stop.
items.why: 'Terminal' sounds like an ending, so students expect the motion to stop rather than to settle at a steady speed. The graph levels off at the terminal velocity: the object keeps falling at that constant velocity because the resultant force is zero.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the unit of acceleration?
items.correct: Metres per second squared, m/s^2.
items.misconception: Acceleration is quoted in metres per second, m/s, the same as velocity.
items.why: The equation contains a velocity in metres per second, and students copy the unit from the numerator rather than working it through the division by time. Acceleration is a change in velocity divided by a time, so its unit is (m/s) / s, which is m/s^2.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student walks 30 m east then 30 m back to the start. Some say the displacement is 30 m. Why is that wrong?
items.correct: Displacement is measured from the start point to the finish point, which here are the same point, so it is zero.
items.misconception: Displacement is the greatest distance the object got from its starting point.
items.why: The furthest point reached is a memorable feature of the journey, and it does describe a straight-line distance, so it looks like a displacement. Displacement depends only on where the object starts and where it ends, not on how far it strayed in between.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
items.correct: The distance travelled, or the displacement, during that time.
items.misconception: The enclosed area is taken to be the acceleration.
items.why: Acceleration is the quantity students associate with velocity-time graphs, so whichever feature of the graph they are asked about, acceleration is the answer that comes to mind first. The area under the line is a velocity multiplied by a time, which is a distance. The acceleration is the gradient, not the area.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
